specPoints.text: know the terms atomic (proton) number, mass (nucleon) number and isotope

primer.text: Every atom of an element carries the same proton count, yet their neutron counts can differ. Such siblings are isotopes. This note defines isotopes, works chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 side by side, and explains why proton-neutron imbalance leaves some isotopes unstable.

lessons.title: Defining isotopes
lessons.opening: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with equal numbers of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Because the proton count fixes the element, isotopes share chemical identity while their nuclei differ in mass.
keyPoints: Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
The proton count determines the element, so isotopes are always the same element.
Isotopes of one element differ only in their neutron count.
Each element can have several isotopes.

low.restatement: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 both have 17 protons. One has 18 neutrons, the other 20 — same element, different nuclei.
low.analogy: Isotopes are like identical twins wearing backpacks of different weights: same person, different load.
low.examPointer: Quote the definition with both halves: same protons, different neutrons. One half alone scores zero.

medium.restatement: Nuclear notation exposes isotopes at a glance: the atomic number is shared, the mass number differs. Neutron number is the difference, so each isotope occupies its own point on the chart of nuclides with its own stability.
medium.analogy: Same house number (protons, the identity), different number of residents (neutrons, the mass).
medium.examPointer: When two notations share a lower number, say the word "isotopes" and justify it with the proton equality.

check.stem: What must two atoms share to be isotopes of the same element?

options.explanation: Proton count fixes the element; isotopes differ only in neutrons.
Differing neutrons is exactly what makes them isotopes.
Mass numbers differ between isotopes.

options.text: the same number of electrons and neutrons
options.explanation: Neutrons differ; electrons are irrelevant to the definition.

check.stem: How do chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 differ?

options.explanation: 35 − 17 = 18 and 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons: a difference of two.
Both have 17 protons — extra protons would change the element.
Neutral atoms of both have 17 electrons.
Shared proton count means the same element.

check.stem: An isotope’s mass number differs from another isotope of the same element because…

options.text: its nucleus holds a different number of neutrons
options.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons; only neutrons vary.

options.text: its nucleus holds a different number of protons
options.explanation: Protons are constant across isotopes.
Electron loss changes charge, not the mass number.
Nuclear size is not what the mass number measures.

check.stem: Which pair of numbers could describe two isotopes of the same element?

options.explanation: Shared atomic number with different mass numbers is the isotope pattern.
Different atomic numbers are different elements.

options.text: atomic number 8, mass numbers 16 and 17 protons
options.explanation: A proton change would alter the atomic number.
Again two elements, not isotopes.

check.stem: Why are isotopes of an element chemically indistinguishable in most reactions?

options.text: because chemistry depends on electrons, and their count tracks the unchanged proton number
options.explanation: Equal protons give equal electrons in neutral atoms, so chemistry matches.
Their masses differ — that is the definition.
Neutrons are chemically inert inside the nucleus.

options.text: because isotopes always decay at the same rate
options.explanation: Decay behaviour differs between isotopes.

check.modelAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

check.stem: State what stays the same and what changes between two isotopes of carbon.
check.modelAnswer: The proton count stays the same (6 for carbon) while the neutron count changes, so the mass number changes too.

check.stem: Explain why an atom with 8 protons and 10 neutrons is an isotope of oxygen rather than a different element.
check.modelAnswer: The proton count of 8 fixes the element as oxygen; the neutron count only selects which isotope of oxygen it is.

check.stem: Two neutral atoms have notations of atomic number 17 with mass numbers 35 and 37. Give the neutron and electron counts for each atom.
check.modelAnswer: Each atom has 17 protons and 17 electrons; the neutrons are 35 − 17 = 18 and 37 − 17 = 20 respectively.

lessons.title: Stability and abundance of isotopes
lessons.opening: Isotopes differ in stability: an imbalance between protons and neutrons leaves some nuclei prone to decay and rare in nature. Hydrogen shows the spread, from common hydrogen-1 to scarce deuterium and vanishingly rare tritium.
keyPoints: Some isotopes are unstable because of a proton-neutron imbalance.
Unstable isotopes are more likely to decay and often rarer in nature.
About 2 in every 10,000 hydrogen atoms are the isotope deuterium.
Tritium is far rarer still — roughly 1 in a billion billion hydrogen atoms.

low.restatement: Hydrogen-1 is the everyday form. Deuterium adds one neutron; tritium adds two and is so rare you will never meet it outside special sources.
low.analogy: Think of stability like a balanced seesaw: the proton-neutron balance keeps some nuclei level, while lopsided ones wobble until they decay.
low.examPointer: Abundance figures are order-of-magnitude facts: deuterium 2 in 10,000; tritium 1 in 10¹⁸. Do not swap them.

medium.restatement: Nuclear stability depends on the proton-to-neutron ratio; departing too far from it raises the nucleus’s energy and its likelihood of decaying. That same imbalance explains why unstable isotopes are less abundant in nature.
medium.analogy: A supermarket shelf: the well-balanced isotope is stocked everywhere (hydrogen-1), the slightly awkward one is a niche product (deuterium), and the unstable one is a discontinued line (tritium).
medium.examPointer: Link the ideas in one sentence for the exam: imbalance → instability → decay → scarcity.

check.stem: What makes some isotopes more unstable than others?

options.text: an imbalance between their protons and neutrons
options.explanation: The proton-neutron balance governs nuclear stability.
Electrons do not affect nuclear stability.
Nuclear stability is not set by atomic size.
Stability is nuclear, not chemical.

check.stem: Which isotope of hydrogen is rarer, deuterium or tritium?

options.explanation: Tritium is about 1 in a billion billion; deuterium is 2 in 10,000.
Deuterium is far more common than tritium.
The abundances differ by many orders of magnitude.
Both occur naturally, in the stated tiny fractions.

check.stem: About 2 in every 10,000 hydrogen atoms are deuterium. What fraction is that?

options.explanation: 2/10,000 simplifies to 1/5,000.
That would be 20 in 10,000 — ten times too high.
That would be 0.2 in 10,000 — ten times too low.
That magnitude belongs to tritium, not deuterium.

check.stem: Why might an unstable isotope be unlikely to occur naturally in large amounts?

options.text: because unstable nuclei decay away over time
options.explanation: Decay converts the isotope into other nuclei, depleting natural stores.

options.text: because it is too chemically reactive to form compounds
options.explanation: The scarcity is nuclear, not chemical.

options.text: because it cannot exist on Earth
options.explanation: Unstable isotopes exist; they simply do not persist.
Decay changes identity, not the argument about abundance.

check.stem: Two isotopes of an element have very different proton-neutron ratios. What else will differ?

options.explanation: Stability, set by the ratio, sets the decay likelihood.

options.text: their position in the periodic table
options.explanation: Both share the same atomic number and so the same position.
The element symbol is shared.

options.text: their electron configuration in neutral atoms
options.explanation: Equal protons mean equal electrons and similar chemistry.

check.stem: Name the two heavier isotopes of hydrogen and state how many neutrons each contains.
check.modelAnswer: Deuterium is hydrogen with one neutron, and tritium is hydrogen with two neutrons.

check.stem: State the approximate natural abundance of deuterium among hydrogen atoms.
check.modelAnswer: Deuterium makes up about 2 in every 10,000 hydrogen atoms.

check.stem: Explain why an isotope with a large proton-neutron imbalance may be less likely to occur naturally.
check.modelAnswer: The imbalance makes the nucleus unstable, so it decays into other nuclei; over time the unstable isotope is depleted and becomes rare in nature.

check.stem: A sample contains 100,000 hydrogen atoms. Estimate how many are deuterium, and name the rarer isotope.
check.modelAnswer: At 2 in 10,000, the sample holds about 20 deuterium atoms; tritium is the rarer isotope.

glossary.definition: An atom of an element with the usual proton count but a different number of neutrons.
The hydrogen isotope containing one neutron (hydrogen-2).
The rare hydrogen isotope containing two neutrons (hydrogen-3).

workedExample.prompt: State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in the two chlorine isotopes with atomic number 17 and mass numbers 35 and 37.
steps: Atomic number 17 means 17 protons, and neutral atoms carry 17 electrons.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Both isotopes: 17 protons, 17 electrons; chlorine-35 has 18 neutrons and chlorine-37 has 20 neutrons.
